messages.author: bc748aaef95ecfa3
messages.subject: Expontential function in linear predictor
parts:
Hello,

I would like to fit the following model using INLA:

Y_{1,i} ~Negbin(mu1,r)
Y_{2,i}~Negbin(mu2,r)
Y_{3,i}~Negbin(mu3,r)
Y_{4,i}~Negbin(mu4,r)

log(mu1)=log(n_i)+log(1-exp(-lambda_i 2^{rho_i}))
log(mu2)=log(n_i)+log(exp(-lambda_i 2^{rho_i})-exp(-lambda_i 10^{rho_i}))
log(mu3)=log(n_i)+log(exp(-lambda_i 2^{rho_i})-exp(-lambda_i 10^{rho_i}))
log(mu3)=log(n_i)+log(exp(-lambda_i 75^{rho_i}))

whereby lambda_i=beta1+beta2*age_i+beta3*I_weekend_i
and rho_i=beta4+beta5*age_i+beta6*I_weekend_i

and the log(n_i) is actually the offset.

Is it possible to do this and do you have any suggestions how to do it?
I have done a model with different linear predictors for each of the response categories, but I do not know how to adapt the formula to the above equations.

Kind regards,
Kim

messages.author: b453c29749de564d
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Expontential function in linear predictor
parts:
your only hope is to use the rgeneric tool, see inla.doc("rgeneric")

make sure to use hyperparameters in a good internal scale (like
log(precision) )

H

Hi,

in your case you'll only need to use the mean-model with a tiny
artificial noise on top of that. I can be that the number of
hyperparameters you'll get, since you have the _i thing, is simply to
much and you'll be better off doing this in another framework. 

Best
H
